title: MATH GAOKAO - 421
description: Authentic-style mathematics problems inspired by China’s Gaokao — build deeper understanding, sharper thinking, and real exam readiness.

questions.concept: Case Split for Quadratic Residues Modulo \(4\)
questions.learningObjective: Choose an appropriate case split to prove that \(n^2\) leaves remainder \(0\) or \(1\) modulo \(4\).
questions.question: To prove by cases that \(n^2\) leaves remainder \(0\) or \(1\) when divided by \(4\) for every integer \(n\), which case split is appropriate?
questions.explanation: Every integer is either even or odd. If \(n=2k\), then \(n^2=4k^2\), which leaves remainder \(0\) modulo \(4\). If \(n=2k+1\), then \(n^2=4k^2+4k+1\), which leaves remainder \(1\) modulo \(4\). These two cases cover all integers. The sign split \(n>0\) and \(n<0\) omits \(n=0\) and does not directly determine the remainder modulo \(4\).
questions.hint: Choose exhaustive cases that make the square easy to reduce modulo the given divisor.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the cases needed to prove that \(n^2\) leaves remainder \(0\) or \(1\) modulo \(3\).
questions.question: To prove by cases that \(n^2\) leaves remainder \(0\) or \(1\) when divided by \(3\) for every integer \(n\), which case split directly classifies the residue of \(n\) modulo \(3\)?
questions.explanation: Division by \(3\) gives exactly three possible remainders: \(0\), \(1\), and \(2\). Thus every integer \(n\) has one of the forms \(3k\), \(3k+1\), or \(3k+2\). Checking these three cases covers all integers. Parity alone is not sufficient to determine remainders modulo \(3\).
questions.hint: List all possible remainders when an integer is divided by \(3\).

questions.concept: Proof by Cases with Absolute Value
questions.learningObjective: Complete the case \(x<0\) in a proof that \(|x|\ge x\) for all real \(x\).
questions.question: In a proof by cases that \(|x|\ge x\) for every real number \(x\), which option correctly completes the case \(x<0\)?

options.label: A
options.text: If \(x<0\), then \(|x|=-x\), and since \(-x<0\), we get \(|x|<x\).

options.label: B
options.text: If \(x<0\), then \(|x|=-x\), and since \(-x>0>x\), we get \(|x|>x\), hence \(|x|\ge x\).

questions.explanation: For \(x<0\), the definition of absolute value gives \(|x|=-x\). Because \(x<0\), we have \(-x>0\), so \(-x>x\). Therefore \(|x|=-x>x\), which implies \(|x|\ge x\). Option A has the wrong sign for \(-x\) when \(x<0\).

questions.concept: Proof by Cases for a Product with an Odd Gap
questions.learningObjective: Verify a parity proof for a product of two integers whose difference is odd.
questions.question: Which option gives a correct proof by cases that \(n(n+7)\) is even for every integer \(n\)? Here \(k\) denotes an integer.

options.label: A
options.text: If \(n=2k\), then \(n(n+7)=2k(2k+7)\), which is even. If \(n=2k+1\), then \(n(n+7)=2(2k+1)(k+4)\), which is odd.

options.label: B
options.text: If \(n=2k\), then \(n(n+7)=2k(2k+7)\), which is even. If \(n=2k+1\), then \(n(n+7)=2(2k+1)(k+4)\), which is even.

questions.explanation:
For even \(n\), the factor \(n\) supplies a factor of \(2\). For odd \(n=2k+1\), the other factor is \(n+7=2k+8=2(k+4)\), so
\[
n(n+7)=2(2k+1)(k+4),
\]
which is also even. The distractor incorrectly calls this explicit multiple of \(2\) odd.
questions.hint: Look for an explicit integer factor of two in each parity case.

questions.concept: Proof by Cases for Absolute Value Squared
questions.learningObjective: Prove by cases that \(|x|^2=x^2\) for every real number \(x\).
questions.question: Which option correctly proves by cases that \(|x|^2=x^2\) for every real number \(x\)?
questions.explanation: For \(x\ge0\), the definition gives \(|x|=x\), hence \(|x|^2=x^2\). For \(x<0\), the definition gives \(|x|=-x\), hence \(|x|^2=(-x)^2=x^2\). Thus both cases give \(|x|^2=x^2\). Option B reverses the definition of absolute value in each case.
questions.hint: Use the definition of \(|x|\) separately for nonnegative and negative \(x\).

questions.concept: Proof by Cases for Nonnegative Squares
questions.learningObjective: Prove by cases that \(x^2\ge0\) for every real number \(x\).
questions.question: Which option correctly proves by cases that \(x^2\ge0\) for every real number \(x\)?

options.label: A
options.text: If \(x\ge0\), then \(x^2\ge0\); if \(x<0\), then \(x\) is negative, so \(x^2<0\).

questions.explanation: If \(x\ge0\), then \(x^2\) is a product of nonnegative numbers, so \(x^2\ge0\). If \(x<0\), then \(-x>0\), and \(x^2=(-x)^2>0\), so again \(x^2\ge0\). Option A incorrectly claims that the square of a negative number is negative.
questions.hint: For a negative \(x\), write \(x^2=(-x)^2\) and note that \(-x\) is positive.

questions.learningObjective: Verify a three-case proof of a cubic congruence modulo three.
questions.question: Which option correctly proves by cases that \(n^3\equiv n\pmod3\) for every integer \(n\)? Here \(k\) denotes an integer.
questions.explanation:
The three cases \(n=3k\), \(n=3k+1\), and \(n=3k+2\) exhaust the integers. Expanding the cubes gives remainders \(0\), \(1\), and \(2\), respectively, matching the remainder of \(n\). In particular,
\[
(3k+2)^3=27k^3+54k^2+36k+8=3(9k^3+18k^2+12k+2)+2.
\]
The distractor changes the final remainder to \(1\), so its last equality is false.
questions.hint: Expand the cube in each residue case and separate the multiple of the modulus.

questions.concept: Case Analysis for Absolute Value Sum
questions.learningObjective: Choose the correct case split to prove \(|x|+|x-2|\ge2\).
questions.question: To prove by cases that \(|x|+|x-2|\ge2\) for every real number \(x\), which case split makes the signs of both \(x\) and \(x-2\) fixed within each case, so that both absolute values can be removed directly?
questions.explanation: The expression \(|x|+|x-2|\) changes form when \(x\) crosses the points where \(x=0\) and \(x-2=0\), that is, \(x=0\) and \(x=2\). Therefore the natural cases are \(x<0\), \(0\le x\le2\), and \(x>2\). The split \(x<0\) and \(x\ge0\) does not distinguish the behavior of \(|x-2|\) for \(x>2\).
questions.hint: Find the values of \(x\) where each absolute value changes sign.

questions.concept: Proof by Cases for Sum of Two Absolute Values
questions.learningObjective: Prove by cases that \(|x-1|+|x-2|\ge1\) for every real number \(x\).
questions.question: Which option correctly proves by cases that \(|x-1|+|x-2|\ge1\) for every real number \(x\)?

options.label: A
options.text: If \(x<1\), the sum is \((1-x)+(2-x)=3-2x>1\); if \(1\le x\le2\), the sum is \((x-1)+(2-x)=1\); if \(x>2\), the sum is \((x-1)+(x-2)=2x-3>1\). Hence the sum is always at least \(1\).

options.label: B
options.text: If \(x<1\), the sum is \((x-1)+(x-2)=2x-3\); if \(1\le x\le2\), the sum is \((1-x)+(2-x)=3-2x\); if \(x>2\), the sum is \((1-x)+(2-x)=3-2x\). Hence the sum is always at least \(1\).

questions.explanation: The sign changes occur at \(x=1\) and \(x=2\), giving three cases. For \(x<1\), both \(x-1\) and \(x-2\) are negative, so the sum is \((1-x)+(2-x)=3-2x\). Since \(x<1\), \(3-2x>1\). For \(1\le x\le2\), the sum is \((x-1)+(2-x)=1\). For \(x>2\), both are positive, so the sum is \((x-1)+(x-2)=2x-3>1\). Thus the sum is always at least \(1\). Option B uses incorrect absolute-value expressions.
questions.hint: Split at \(x=1\) and \(x=2\), then determine the sign of each expression inside the absolute values.

questions.concept: Proof by Cases for Odd Expression
questions.learningObjective: Prove by parity cases that \(n^2+n+1\) is odd for every integer \(n\).
questions.question: Which option correctly proves by cases that \(n^2+3n+5\) is odd for every integer \(n\)? Here \(k\) denotes an integer.

options.label: A
options.text: If \(n=2k\), then \(n^2+3n+5=2(2k^2+3k+2)+1\), which is odd. If \(n=2k+1\), then \(n^2+3n+5=2(2k^2+5k+4)+1\), which is odd.

options.label: B
options.text: If \(n=2k\), then \(n^2+3n+5=2(2k^2+3k+2)\), which is even. If \(n=2k+1\), then \(n^2+3n+5=2(2k^2+5k+4)\), which is even.

questions.explanation:
Substitution gives
\[
(2k)^2+3(2k)+5=4k^2+6k+5=2(2k^2+3k+2)+1
\]
and
\[
(2k+1)^2+3(2k+1)+5=4k^2+10k+9=2(2k^2+5k+4)+1.
\]
Each result is one more than an even integer. The distractor drops the final \(+1\) in both cases.
questions.hint: Substitute the two parity forms, expand, and inspect the remainder after factoring out two.
